title: Never too late
hook: many adults celebrate a bar or bat mitzvah later in life

segments.voice: Yesterday your line was teach at thirteen: a young person reads the Torah, then turns around and teaches. Who heard your three sentences? Today, the same moment, arriving late. Day one thousand three hundred one.

Water drips onto a stone at the mouth of a well. Drip. Drip. Over years it has worn a hollow into it. A man named Akiva stands looking at it. He has never learned to read. Not one letter. He's a grown man, and tradition says he's forty years old. And standing there he thinks: if soft water can carve hard stone, then surely the words of Torah, which are strong as iron, can carve a heart that is only flesh. He goes home, takes his young son by the hand, and the two of them sit down with the children's teacher to learn the alphabet. Today's line is what the stone told him.
screen: `WATER ON A STONE.` → `A GROWN MAN WHO CAN'T READ.` → `FATHER AND SON LEARN THE ALPHABET.`

segments.voice: Never too late. Turn it four ways. First, Akiva. The story is told in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an early rabbinic collection. The man who started at forty, sitting with the children over the alphabet, became, in the tradition's memory, one of its great teachers. The rabbis didn't hide his late start. They kept it in the story. Second, Abraham. Genesis says Abraham was ninety-nine when he entered the covenant of circumcision, the covenant we met earlier this week, the one a baby receives at eight days old. Abraham himself came to it as an old man. Third, today. Some adults never had a bar or bat mitzvah. Their family wasn't observant, or the ceremony wasn't offered to girls where they grew up, or life simply got in the way. Now some synagogues run adult classes, and a group studies together, sometimes for a long stretch, and then stands up together to read from the Torah. A retired engineer learning the melody of the reading alongside a young nurse. Fourth, what it shows. Two days ago we saw that by law, a person becomes bar or bat mitzvah with age, ceremony or not. So the adult ceremony isn't a status earned late. It's a choice made late: to stand up, to read, to teach, in front of everyone, because they want to. Water, given time, gets through stone.
screen: `AKIVA STARTS AT FORTY.` · `ABRAHAM AT NINETY-NINE.` · `ADULTS STAND UP TOGETHER.` · `A CHOICE, MADE LATE.` · then, large: `NEVER TOO LATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: start one late thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you once wanted to learn or do and decided you'd missed your chance. An instrument. A language. A faith practice. A degree. A friendship you let lapse. Picture Akiva at the well, watching the water. Now name the smallest first letter of that thing. Not the whole path. The alef. One lesson, one phone call, one page. Hold it. If you pray, you can ask for patience to begin. The bell holds the time.
Never too late. Akiva learning his letters beside his son, Abraham's covenant at ninety-nine, and adults standing up to read. Today's word.
Your line: never too late. Today, take the first small step you named: the one lesson, the one call, the one page. Day one thousand three hundred one.

howItsDone: Some synagogues offer adult bar and bat mitzvah classes: a group studies together and then reads from the Torah together, often including people who never had the ceremony as children.
